entry.title: The Security+ PKI Chain of Trust, Link by Link
entry.summary: Most Security+ certificate questions tend to revolve around the same basic idea: pinpointing where the chain breaks. Once the chain can be traced from memory, the PKI portion of objective 1.4 shrinks a lot. A website's certificate isn't trusted by itself. It was signed by an intermediate CA, and that intermediate was signed by a root CA. The browser or OS has the root preloaded in its trust store, and that root is the foundation of trust, the starting point for every verification. Upon connecting, the client reviews the chain. It ensures the server certificate was signed by the intermediate, and that the intermediate was signed by a root the client already has. It also checks for any expiration or revocation along the way. If all steps are valid, the connection is trusted. If any step fail…

entry.title: Another Day, Another Bot Attack: The Reality of Running an Indie Site
entry.summary: Today was one of those days every indie site owner dreads. For three straight hours, SiteToolsBox.com was hammered by a bot wave. Fake submissions, spam comments, and automated tool flooding — the works. From the moment I opened the analytics dashboard, the numbers looked wrong: traffic spiked from nowhere, submission forms were filling themselves, and comment sections were being flooded with garbage. It’s exhausting. You spend months building something useful, polishing the UI, tweaking the weight scoring system, and adding features like favorites and featured listings — only to wake up to a script kiddie’s playground. Here is what happened today: 3 hours of continuous automated submissions from rotating IPs Comment moderation queue with pending/approved/rejected states If you’re building something in public, expect this. It’s not a matter of if you get spammed, but when. The key is having the tools to fight back without burning out.

entry.title: AI-Generated Code Can Look Correct and Still Be Wrong
entry.summary: AI coding tools have made writing code faster. But one of the biggest mistakes developers can make is assuming that code which looks correct is actually correct. AI is very good at producing code that looks clean, follows familiar patterns, and seems reasonable at first glance. The problem is that code doesn't just need to look good. It needs to work within the context of the entire application. AI might generate a function that: Handles the happy path perfectly. Uses the correct syntax. Looks clean and readable. Passes a quick visual inspection. But it might still fail because of an edge case, an incorrect assumption, a missing validation, or a side effect somewhere else in the system. This is where blindly trusting AI-generated code becomes dangerous. Even when an AI tool has access to your codebase, it may not fully understand: Why a particular architectural decision was made. Which parts of the system depend on a function. What assumptions your database or API relies on. What could break if a seemingly small change is introduced. The code may solve the immediate problem while creating a different one. I think the best workflow isn't: Ask AI → Copy code → Move on. It's: Ask AI → Review the approach → Test assumptions → Verify the code → Integrate. AI can help write the code, explain unfamiliar logic, suggest edge cases, and speed up debugging. But the responsibility for understanding what gets shipped still belongs to the developer. The biggest benefit of AI coding tools isn't that developers no longer need to think. It's that we can spend less time on repetitive implementation and more time on architecture, debugging, reviewing decisions, and solving the actual problem. AI can generate code in seconds. Knowing whether that code belongs in your system is still an engineering skill. Use AI to write code faster. Don't use it as a replacement for understanding your code.
